answer.sourceLine: This is a real passage from the Meditations, Book IV, section 23 — in the English of George Long, whose translation was published in London in 1862. The wording that circulates online is Long’s Victorian phrasing, confirmed word for word in the scanned 1862 text and in Project Gutenberg’s edition of the same translation.

source.excerpt: Everything harmonizes with me, which is harmonious to thee, O Universe. Nothing for me is too early nor too late, which is in due time for thee. Everything is fruit to me which thy seasons bring, O Nature: from thee are all things, in thee are all things, to thee all things return. The poet says, Dear city of Cecrops; and wilt not thou say, Dear city of Zeus?
trail: Searched Quote Investigator’s Marcus Aurelius files ↗ first; there is no investigation of this line, which is consistent with it being an unremarkable, genuine passage rather than a contested one.

Read the scanned Bell and Daldy edition of 1862 ↗, whose title page reads “Translated by George Long · London: Bell and Daldy, Fleet Street · 1862”. Section 23 of Book IV carries the wording exactly, “nor” and all.
Cross-checked the same section in Project Gutenberg’s text of Long’s translation ↗ and in the Internet Classics Archive Book IV ↗, which reproduces Long unnumbered.
Confirmed the book and section independently against C. R. Haines’s Greek-and-English Loeb edition of 1916 ↗, where section 23 of Book IV is the same passage in different English.
source.excerptNote: The quotation as it circulates usually stops at “O Nature”. The rest of section 23 — the return of all things, and the exchange about the “dear city” — is where Marcus turns the thought outward.

source.rightsNote: Marcus’s Greek original is ancient and long out of copyright, and the English shown here is George Long’s translation, published in London in 1862 — far earlier than 1931, so it is public domain in the United States. Note that this applies to Long’s wording specifically: modern translations of the same passage, such as Gregory Hays’s or Maxwell Staniforth’s, are separate works and are not covered by that status.

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus was born at Rome on 26 April AD 121 and ruled as emperor from 161 until his death in 180. The book we call Meditations was never a book to him: it is a set of private notebooks written in Greek, addressed to himself, full of reminders to accept what happens and to keep his own judgement clean. Because it was written for an audience of one, it reads less like philosophy for publication than like a man arguing himself back into calm.

misattribution.heading: What gets it wrong
misattribution.intro: The author is right. Almost everything else about how this line travels is not — the book number, one word of the wording, and the silent assumption that this is Marcus’s own English.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ lists this sentence under its Book XII heading with the citation “XII, 30”, welded onto the start of a different passage. In Long’s translation, section 30 of Book XII actually begins “There is one light of the sun, though it is interrupted by walls, mountains, and other things infinite” — the harmony sentence is at Book IV, 23 ↗.

Sites that scrape Wikiquote reproduce the same citation: LibQuotes ↗, for instance, files it as Meditations, Book XII, Section 30. The wrong location has been copied far more often than the right one.
The version that circulates usually swaps in “or”. Long’s 1862 text ↗ reads “Nothing for me is too early nor too late”.

Marcus wrote in Greek; the “thee” and “thou” are George Long’s Victorian idiom. C. R. Haines’s 1916 Loeb translation ↗ gives the same section as “All that is in tune with thee, O Universe, is in tune with me!”

misattribution.truthLine: The quote is genuinely Marcus Aurelius — Meditations, Book IV, section 23, in George Long’s 1862 translation ↗, not Book XII.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The line is Marcus talking himself out of impatience. He is not saying the world is kind — he is saying that his own sense of timing has no standing against the order of things, so whatever arrives, arrives on time. The Stoic move is to relocate the word “early” from the universe (where it does not apply) to his own wanting (where it does).

The passage does not stop where the internet stops it. Long’s section 23 runs on: “from thee are all things, in thee are all things, to thee all things return. The poet says, Dear city of Cecrops; and wilt not thou say, Dear city of Zeus?” Having accepted nature’s timing, Marcus widens the idea of citizenship from a single city to the whole cosmos — a pointed thought from a man who had spent much of his reign away from Rome.
context.detailsSummary: How different translators render the same Greek
detailsBody: The archaic “thee” and “thou” belong to George Long, not to Marcus, who wrote in Greek. Long’s 1862 English is the version that became the internet standard, largely because it is out of copyright and easy to reproduce.

C. R. Haines rendered the same section in the 1916 Loeb Classical Library edition as: “All that is in tune with thee, O Universe, is in tune with me! Nothing that is in due time for thee is too early or too late for me! All that thy seasons bring, O Nature, is fruit for me! All things come from thee, subsist in thee, go back to thee.” Same passage, same numbering, quite different music — a useful reminder that a “quote” from an ancient author is always also a quote from a translator.
